title: The left and right agree on one thing: no data centers
excerpt: Florida’s data center bans are part of a bigger, broader, and bipartisan revolt against the AI industry.
content_html:
Today, I’m talking with Gaby Del Valle, a policy reporter here at The Verge, about the growing backlash against AI data centers.

Gaby recently reported a fantastic piece about Hernando County, Florida, where last month the county commission unanimously approved a yearlong moratorium on data center construction. She attended a protest there organized by a group called Humans First, a conservative grassroots movement focused on combating AI data center build-outs.

You’ll hear Gaby explain that it was part of a bigger, broader, and bipartisan opposition to data centers. Not only as physical buildings, but as infrastructure that powers an AI boom that takes local jobs and fills feeds with slop.

Data center construction has become a proxy for the public’s feelings about AI: something physical they can aim their fear and frustration at — and even create enough pressure to stop through community organizing and protests.

So I wanted Gaby to talk me through what these protests look like on the ground, from voters whose party affiliations have typically aligned them with big business. You’ll hear Gaby say data centers are scrambling party lines, turning diehard Trump voters into protesters who care about left-coded issues like groundwater contamination and forever chemicals.

It’s a confusing time, and data centers are going to play a major role in electoral politics going forward. So I suspect this won’t be the last we hear from Gaby on movements like Humans First.

Okay: Verge policy reporter Gaby Del Valle on the bipartisan data center backlash. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Gaby Del Valle, you’re a policy reporter here at The Verge. Welcome back to Decoder.

Thank you. Happy to be here.

I’m excited to talk to you. You were on previously with our friend Alex Heath, but this is the first time I’ve gotten to talk to you in Decoder. I think the story you just wrote about data centers and conservative backlash in Florida is just a real preview of what tech policy going into the midterm elections is going to be like.

You were just there. You talked to a bunch of people who are protesting data centers. It is a real alignment scramble in terms of our politics. Tell us what you found.

What I found was people are really, really, really, really mad. And the reasons why they’re mad are different depending on the community, but they’re also all the same, if that makes sense. They have localized concerns. They were telling me Florida’s really humid. It doesn’t make sense to build a data center that needs to be kept very cool and dry in such a humid place. A lot of them were concerned about their groundwater. They were concerned about PFAS getting dumped into the water.

But I’ve also talked to people in Arizona who have the opposite concern. Arizona is not very humid. Arizona’s very dry. And they’re also like, “It doesn’t make sense to build a data center in the desert.” So whatever your community is, you’re like, “It doesn’t make sense to build a data center here because of X reason,” basically.

The thing that really strikes me in reading your piece and hearing about the other reporting you’re doing for pieces to come is that data center build-outs and data center protests do not neatly map to the usual right-left culture war alignment that we have seen play out for so long. And I’m curious about your view on that. Why can’t Elon Musk just command his army of followers to be pro-data centers?

This is so interesting to me. So this is a little bit of backstory that’s going to answer your question. The woman who organized Humans First, which was bipartisan and now is focusing only on organizing conservatives, was an early founder or organizer with the Tea Party way back when. And this has a similar vibe to me. It’s not a left-right thing. It’s a populous technocrat divide.

You’re seeing that on the right and the left. So for example, at the Abundance Conference last year, it was center-right to center-left-ish. And everybody was pro-nuclear, pro-AI. And we were hearing that, “These things are here to stay. We have to figure out how to do it smartly.” At the same time, the populist left and the populist right are both skeptical of tech development, to put it lightly.

That skepticism plays out across a number of dimensions. I couldn’t help but be struck as I read your story by how many strains of conspiracy thinking there are about data centers.

I’m curious if they’re just visible. They’re so big, and they require so much development and so much build-out that you can just glue any concerns you have onto them. “This big thing is happening, and I don’t feel any control. And I’m also worried about 5G, Chinese government interference, and X, Y, Z. And I can just point it all at this very big thing by which there’s a process to say no. I can go to my local town board meeting and literally say no.”

I mean, I think that’s part of it. It’s interesting because I think there’s a spectrum of conspiratorial thinking to, I guess, misinformed thinking on the water use question. We now know that they don’t use as much water as we previously thought, et cetera, et cetera. But on the far end of the spectrum, one of the people I talked to told me that cattle born near data centers are all stillborn. I tried to track that down. I was like, “Where did this come from?” And it was one farmer in Texas who claims he had one stillborn calf on his cattle farm.

So that got spun out via the internet rumor, social media mill. I think that’s part of it. There’s this issue of social collapse that comes out once you talk to people a little bit. One of the women I talked to said, “I had this friend. ChatGPT told her she couldn’t be friends with me anymore.” You have all of these stories of people harming themselves, going off their medication, or whatever because they’ve been talking to a chatbot and it goes awry.

I think this gives people a feeling of control. Where I can go to my community board meeting or my council members’ meeting, and I can say, “I don’t want this big building that houses the scary thing that is fracturing my community here.” So it’s not just the actual building. I think it’s a broader backlash to generative AI and to LLMs specifically.

One of my ideas that I’ve been pushing on lately is that the AI products are not winning over hearts and minds in the market. So if the data centers just said Netflix on them, maybe people would like them more.

But instead, that’s where the slop is coming from, and it’s why the jobs are going to go away. It’s also where Mark Zuckerberg is just going to get even wealthier. Is there a dynamic of that — that people just don’t like the thing that the data centers make?

Yes, absolutely. They don’t like a lot of the things that the data centers make. It’s not just AI. I think AI is a big part of it, but this is a little preview of a different story I’m working on... In Tucson, there’s a data center project that’s getting built out. The people I talked to there said, “Yeah, this might be an Amazon Web Services facility, and Amazon works with ICE.” So this technology is fueling mass deportations through, not directly, but creating the non-sexy infrastructure that surveillance is built on.

There are two things to it. Part of it is a NIMBY, “I don’t want this thing in my backyard, literally. I don’t want my town to get polluted. I don’t want this. I don’t want that. I don’t want to see it. I don’t want the noise pollution.” And then the other part is, “I do not like what this big building represents and what it has wrought on society.”

Does that cut across bipartisan lines? Or is that more culture war coded?

It’s both. It cuts across culture war lines in that people have different concerns about what LLMs do. So one woman I spoke to was talking about the fracturing of social bonds. On the construction front, she was like, “We’re a rural-ish community. We don’t want this big blight on our nice rolling hills.” So that’s a right-coded thing. And there was a lot of anti-development stuff that is neither right nor left.

On the left, I would say there’s similar culture war concerns, but it’s... I don’t know if this is necessarily a culture war concern, but fueling deportations. Both sides, I think, are concerned about the job losses because of AI. And both sides have caught on to the fact that these facilities don’t really have a lot of long-term job prospects. There’s the big construction boom. There’s an HVAC situation. But to actually maintain these facilities, it doesn’t require that many people.

I think people have caught onto that. The promises of the AI data job, or that the AI boom will lead to jobs related to data centers, are not actually true.

Yeah. At most, it’s a few hundred jobs for each of these facilities, at least in the data centers we have now. Why do you think some of the protests make national news? The Kevin O’Leary data center in Utah is a national story. Maybe it’s just because he’s a cartoon character.

And then there’s a new project in Georgia where there might be a huge OpenAI facility that seems to go under the radar. There are all of the projects in Florida that you are reporting on, but don’t seem to be explosive in the way that some of the other ones are.

Yeah, I think that’s a good question. There was one in Florida that was explosive, and it was just because it was near Mar-a-Lago. I think that one pretty obviously made the national news because it’s related to the president. I honestly think a cartoon character at the center of it is the deciding factor a lot of the time on whether it’ll become a national story or not. And then also the numbers. The Utah one, I don’t remember off the top of my head how big it’s supposed to be, but it’s supposed to be huge. So then that becomes a proxy for all data center development.

They’re being planned everywhere. And I think what’s so interesting is that the backlash exists everywhere too. I relied a lot on, for example, the Tampa Bay Times to figure out the background for this story. They’re on top of it. They’re going to these meetings and watching people get yelled at and asked, “Did you sign an NDA? Yes or no?“

Do you think the local governments are being responsive? You’ve now gone to some of these protests; you’ve talked to people on the ground in various counties across the country. The basic unit of democracy is supposed to be your local government because you know those people and you can yell at them in the grocery store and the town board meeting.

We’re seeing there’s a wall going up in some of these cases where the local governments are saying, “No, we have to do this development. This is the only economic development available.” And the people are saying, “No, we’re going to throw you out.” Do you think local governments on the whole are being responsive or not responsive at all?

I think it really depends. In Hernando County, they did pass a moratorium. There are a lot of counties in Florida where moratoriums have passed. But in Tucson, again, the city government is responsive to what the people want and the county government isn’t, and they’re at odds with each other. There are all these videos of people yelling at their representatives about NDAs again. And then them being like, “We cannot say whether we signed an NDA,” which is an answer, but whatever.

I think it really depends on a lot of things. How small the communities are, for one. How vulnerable the people in office feel to getting voted out, I think, is another big one. In Florida, the Republican primary for governor, I think, might be affected by this issue. The primary is in a few weeks and the front-runner, Byron Donalds, has taken a lot of money from the AI industry and data center development groups. And people are mad. People are really mad.

He was endorsed by Trump, and everyone I spoke to, as proud Trump voters, said things like, “I don’t understand why Trump would endorse him. I’m not going to vote for him.” One woman I talked to who told me she was opposed to everything Democrat said she would vote for a Democrat or an independent if Donalds won the primary. And Donalds has also changed… not his stance on data center development, but the way that he talks about it in response to a lot of this backlash.

How has he changed the stance? How is he talking about it now?

He says his vision is to make Florida the financial capital of the world. And to a lot of people, that would sound great, but these people are really upset by this, both because they... I mean, there are a lot of other things at play here. Housing costs in Florida have gone up exponentially. Not only in big cities like Miami, but in the suburbs of Tampa, for example. Housing prices have shot up to levels that I, as somebody who grew up there, just don’t understand. I literally can’t wrap my head around it.

So I think a lot of the backlash to development and to data centers is also related to people’s cost of living going up and to these, in their words, outside developers coming in and changing a community that’s already changing. He has since said that we need data center development, but we need to do it responsibly.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is another great example of this. He supported a bill that would require data centers to pay their own utilities and also let counties require them to use reclaimed water, which would address the water issue. But the Tampa Bay Times reported that he also supported legislation that gives massive tax breaks to data centers. And that he pushed to amend that law, which I think was signed in 2017, to only apply to hyperscale data centers, which are the ones that people have problems with.

The people I talk to, they know that there are currently data centers in Florida, and they’re smaller. There are no hyperscale data centers, but there are around one hundred smaller ones for Netflix or whatever. And they’re okay with that. One woman I talked to works in IT. She said, “I understand that data centers are a boogeyman, and we need them for stuff. But I don’t want this massive facility using all of our power, emitting these frequencies, et cetera, et cetera.” Another thing that I think is really interesting-

Wait, can you just explain what “emitting these frequencies” means?

[Laughs] Just the noise. I talked to these guys at the Border Security Expo who work for a data center company, and they all live in Virginia. Even they were like, “Yeah, it sucks.” They said, “I hate walking around my neighborhood because I just hear it all the time.” And they work in data centers. I don’t think she meant 5G.

It’s a real element of this, right next to China being a villain of whatever persuasion you need China to be a villain for. Again, there’s just a piece of all this where it’s a big thing that you can stop. The power of NIMBYism can stop this. Maybe we can’t stop everything else. We can’t stop Facebook from doing targeted advertising that feels like it’s listening to you. No one knows how to stop this. It’s bad. We don’t like it, but no one knows how to stop it.

“I can stop this building from being built” seems like it not only scrambles our culture war lines, but it’s scrambling politics, too. Byron Donalds saying he wants Florida to be the financial capital of the world. One, it’s very funny in that he has to contend with the existence of New York, London, Beijing, and Amsterdam. Go down the line.

There are a lot of places that can compete for that title where Miami might not be in the running. But doing it via building data centers is not the path to that result. It’s just a bunch of economic development that might result in some short-term gains.

It feels like people have clocked it, and they’ve clocked that it’s a thing you can stop. I’m curious if there’s anything else. You’ve spent a lot of time covering the right, and I wonder if there’s anything else that scrambles the lines like that. Because in almost every other case, “let’s build stuff, let’s tear down the White House and build a ballroom” is fine. Building things is better, and it is coded in one side of the culture war.

Yeah. I mean, this is, again, so Florida specific, but it really surprised me how much of the politics around this were scrambled. One of the women was talking about this ballot initiative that’s going to pass. It’s going to give more tax exemptions to homeowners, which I feel is a standard Republican thing — lower taxes for homeowners. People would like that.

She said, “This is terrible. It’s going to deprive county governments of funds that they would otherwise get from homeowners, which will then entice the counties even further to have data centers come into our communities.” So she was thinking of the second- and third-order effects of this, even though that’s a pretty populist initiative. But yeah, it’s all so scrambled.

How do you see the scramble inside of the right and then carrying over to the populist left? The idea that a bunch of billionaires threw all of their weight behind Donald Trump in 2024, and that led to, I don’t know, a bunch of podcast bros throwing their weight behind Donald Trump in 2024. There was a cultural wave of Peter Thiel, Marc Andreessen, Elon Musk, and the All-In podcast about building and tech and the future. It feels like that has come to one kind of end.

I don’t think that that wave is driving the culture anymore because of the backlash to AI. We can all see the college students booing at graduation. If the backlash is there against the data centers, against AI taking the jobs, against billionaires in general, what does that turn into on the right? Because that was the animating force of the right for so long.

I think that is still an open question. I think the question is whether this backlash is strong enough to shake people’s other partisan concerns.

If you’ve got a Democrat candidate who is anti-data center development, but also not super gung-ho about deputizing all Florida police officers to do ICE arrests, where does that leave someone who supports Trump’s immigration policies but doesn’t want a data center in their neighborhood? I don’t know. I think that’s what the party is struggling with right now.

I mean, I think Trump is this perfect avatar for people because he somehow stands for anti-elite sentiment, but also for hard work and capitalism. He’s just this perfect blend of, I don’t even know how to describe it. He contains multitudes, I guess. And nobody else can contain multitudes like him. They don’t have the juice. They just don’t have it.

Can I make the argument?

Yeah.

I think I can make the argument. I grew up in Wisconsin, which has many similar dynamics to maybe Florida, in that people in Wisconsin remember a time when there were big factories. In the town I grew up in, Racine, there used to be a Case factory that made tractors. There was a Chrysler factory in Kenosha that made Jeep Wranglers. This is a real thing that occurred, and all those things are gone.

So Trump would promise all of this huge economic development that basically looked like manufacturing. I think what his version of this, even with tariffs, was, “We will bring manufacturing back to all of these places. And that manufacturing will require a lot of hard work, but there will be dignity in that hard work.”

At the end of it, you’re going to get to point to a Modine air conditioner and be like, “I made that thing. My community made that thing.” I think that is very seductive. I mean, Trump spent years promising that we would build iPhones in America, and that’s Wisconsin and Foxconn and all this stuff.

Maybe none of those things were ever going to come true because that’s not how anything gets made anymore. And that’s not even the kind of work people actually want to do in America anymore. But you take all of that energy, and you’re like, “Actually, what we’re going to make is data centers.” And no one can see at the end of that, “I made a Jeep Wrangler.” They get to see that Elon Musk got richer; they just lost their jobs, their children feel like they have no future, and their feeds are full of slop.

And I feel like something gets disconnected in the multitudes where you can tell everyone, “Yeah, the best I can do for you is make you the world’s richest factory foreman.” So people are like, “That sounds awesome. That’s better than whatever nonsense I’m doing online.” But you can’t be like, “I’m going to make Sam Altman richer,” because that doesn’t mean anything to anyone. All of this construction doesn’t do anything for anyone.

I look at the backlash, and all I see is that a lot of people across the political spectrum have come to that realization. You can tear down our communities to build bridges and factories, and you can pollute the skies with smokestacks as long as we all get jobs. But if you’re going to do all that and all I get is more AI-generated movie posters on Amazon Prime whose price keeps going up every month, screw you. And I’m wondering if that connection is... That’s my guess. I’m wondering if you see any hints of that connection in your reporting as you talk to all these people.

I think so. I think the Florida version of making a Jeep Wrangler is like, there were orange groves and cattle ranches, and now there are not. I used to drive past an orange grove when I was a kid. That orange grove is gone. It’s a Publix now. There was an old cow field. Now that’s a mall.

On the one hand, that’s what people want. People want consumption, but they also, at least in Florida, liked thinking that they lived near an orange grove. Like, “Oh, maybe the guy’s using tons of pesticides. Maybe the orange grove is worse for your health than the data center.” I don’t know. I don’t have the stats on this. But you could see the tangible effects of what your economy was producing.

Now it’s just like, “There’s a building that none of us can go in. It makes a horrible noise. And I think it’s drinking all my water?” And then it’s also making your kids dumb and alienated, and making everybody lose their jobs. People don’t like that.

Again, these aren’t Luddites. The woman I talked to said, “I found out about the Humans First organizing [efforts] via Facebook. I know there’s an irony in that. I know there’s an irony in me working in IT and opposing this data center.” They’re not dumb. They understand that all of these things that we’ve built our lives around require something to power them. They just don’t want that something to be within driving distance of their house. They want it somewhere else.

And it’s unclear where that somewhere else should be apart from space.

Apart from space.

That is a very different episode of Decoder. But that’s one answer the industry has: “These people, their stupid concerns are too annoying. We’ll just put the data centers in space,” and maybe they’ll solve that problem. Who knows?

The other answer is, “We’ll just horsepower over their concerns. This is too important. We’re going to do it anyway. And maybe we’ll just subsidize a bunch of education in some community. Maybe we’ll just pay a bunch of extra money. Maybe we’ll pay for everyone’s electricity.”

I don’t know if those have gotten any traction. Is there anything that the tech companies or the neoclouds could do in these communities to overcome the objections? Could they just pay for healthcare? Or is that just a non-starter?

I don’t know about paying for healthcare, but something that I didn’t include in the piece, because it was extremely dry and very technical, was that the small protest ended with about an hour and a half long presentation from a land use expert on how to write local zoning ordinances to prevent hyperscale data centers from being built. It was really specific stuff, like “You could have them on multiple small parcels of land.” It was really dry. “You could require them to use this amount of reclaimed water, et cetera, et cetera.”

I think what people want more than the data centers not being there is a degree of community input on how they’re built — if they’re going to be built. I think if they got that, they would maybe not be pacified, but they would at least not feel like there’s a big external force coming in and steamrolling their community, especially when they already feel like that in every other aspect of their life.

This is the thing that I’m most curious about. So much of our politics and our culture has been nationalized. Everything happens at the national level. The fact that the mayor of New York is a national political figure is at once very silly and also just the funniest thing that has happened in a long time.

Data centers are very local. They’re happening to people in their backyards, and a data center being built in Florida, Georgia, or Tucson has nothing to do with me in New York. It’s far away enough.

Maybe what you’re hearing from everybody is just, “Somewhere else, and as we get to somewhere else, I won’t care.” But it is very local. And then it is very in person. People are going to the meetings; they’re encountering one another. There have been stories of bridges across party lines from people who would never like each other normally because they both hate the data centers.

Is there an element of a return to actual local politics and actual community building here that could be catalyzed by opposition to data centers?

I really think so. Again, I’m talking to organizers in multiple states who are going to these community, town council, or county council meetings and yelling at their representatives. And sometimes it’s hundreds of people. I think this is maybe a weird analogy, but it reminds me of the local backlash to right-wing organizing and local education policy, which is where a lot of the anti-trans backlash started. You’d go into the school board, and you’d be like, “I don’t want this gender stuff being taught to my child. I don’t want my kids to know that slavery was bad.”

I’m not comparing them in terms of value judgment. I just think it’s at a level of local engagement that is at the same time a national issue. It’s these really, really, really localized policies that may end up driving, if not national policy change and national policy discussions, but at least national political vibes. Whoever wins the Democratic and Republican primaries and runs for president in 2028, what are they going to be saying about data centers? I don’t know, but I know it’s going to be informed by what happens this year and next year.

I’m actually very curious how Trump handles it. As you said, he contains multitudes. He’s very good at reading his own base. It feels like the Trump base is very much polarized around data centers. There are a lot of people who love Donald Trump but hate data centers. And then there’s his money, which loves the AI build-out and loves data centers. That is a fracture as deep as anything.

A lot of those folks will say, “AI just has a marketing problem. If only we could convince people of the benefits of this build-out and the super intelligence to come, they would be on board.”

The best marketer they could have for that would be Donald Trump. But he doesn’t seem to be willing to make those claims at the level that they might need. And certainly he is very attuned to his base hating AI. How do you think he’s going to play it? And how do you think the MAGA coalition will respond to it?

Okay, so do you remember when Trump was talking about H-1B visas? Or not even when he was talking about it, but just the whole swirl around what we’re going to do about these?

Yeah.

Trump said, “I think we should stamp an H-1B visa to every foreign student’s college graduation diploma.” And I thought, “What are you talking about? Your administration is charging $100,000 for these visas.” He kept saying things like, “These kids are really smart. We need them in America building chips.”

I think he’s just going to do it like that. The thing about Trump is that he can say literally whatever, and he can do literally whatever, and the people who like him will continue to like him. Sometimes they’ll be like, “Oh, well, I don’t like this particular policy of his. I don’t know why he endorsed this candidate,” but they’re still going to back the guy.

But enough to split the difference on this issue? In every other issue, he could polarize the electorate, and he would get there, but, “I’m going to put a data center in the backyard, and it’s going to make that noise.” Maybe not enough.

But the thing is that they don’t see it as coming from Trump. They’re thinking, “These companies are coming into our community.” And if you connect the dots, it’s like, “Who supports those companies? The president. Who is giving the president a lot of money? All these different companies.”

That’s not how people see it. They see it as these tech oligarchs who are just disconnected from politics and disconnected from anything because of all their money. They don’t see that as having a connection to the president. Instead, they see that as having a connection to the governor, to the board of commissioners, or whatever. But Trump is floating above it all. I don’t know why.

Well, I’m curious, and maybe we should end it here. The Florida gubernatorial primaries are coming up. If Donalds loses, even with that Trump endorsement over the data center issue, do you think that will be a signal or a predictor of what will happen in the midterms?

I think it would be a massive signal, if only because Donalds is polling so much further ahead than everybody else. He’s the clear frontrunner, and the lieutenant governor who’s polling second is also pro-data centers. If any of the anti-data center candidates win the Republican primary, that is going to be huge and completely unexpected by everybody in the state. But it could happen. Crazier things have happened.

We’re going to be doing a lot of coverage of this in the months to come, especially ahead of the midterms, because this scrambling of party lines, this scrambling of the culture war, seems very important. The politics we’ve had for so long, they don’t seem like they can hold up to everyone hating the same thing.

Maybe that’s all America needs. It does seem like every American hating these big buildings that make loud noises might be the thing that unifies us, which is good or bad. You can make your own decisions, but I can’t think of anything else. There’s nothing else that’s cutting across party lines this way. Can you?

Literally nothing. Nothing at all. And it’s cutting across party lines, I think, not just in that people hate it, but I had these deeply conservative women talking to me about local environmental and ecological issues. They were talking about pesticides and forever chemicals in their water, which you wouldn’t expect looking at Republican politics five to 10 years ago, that this is where we have ended up.

We’re still doing climate change hoaxes at the national level, and on the ground we’re talking about pesticides. There’s something there.

Gaby, we’re going to have to have you back as the story develops and certainly as we go into all these elections. Thank you so much for being at Decoder.

Yeah, thanks for having me. This was fun.

Happy to be here.I’m excited to talk to you. You were on previously with our friend Alex Heath, but this is the first time I’ve gotten to talk to you in Decoder. I think the story you just wrote about data centers and conservative backlash in Florida is just a real preview of what tech policy going into the midterm elections is going to be like.You were just there. You talked to a bunch of people who are protesting data centers. It is a real alignment scramble in terms of our politics. Tell us what you found.What I found was people are really, really, really, really mad. And the reasons why they’re mad are different depending on the community, but they’re also all the same, if that makes sense. They have localized concerns. They were telling me Florida’s really humid. It doesn’t make sense to build a data center that needs to be kept very cool and dry in such a humid place. A lot of them were concerned about their groundwater. They were concerned about PFAS getting dumped into the water.But I’ve also talked to people in Arizona who have the opposite concern. Arizona is not very humid. Arizona’s very dry. And they’re also like, “It doesn’t make sense to build a data center in the desert.” So whatever your community is, you’re like, “It doesn’t make sense to build a data center here because of X reason,” basically.The thing that really strikes me in reading your piece and hearing about the other reporting you’re doing for pieces to come is that data center build-outs and data center protests do not neatly map to the usual right-left culture war alignment that we have seen play out for so long. And I’m curious about your view on that. Why can’t Elon Musk just command his army of followers to be pro-data centers?This is so interesting to me. So this is a little bit of backstory that’s going to answer your question. The woman who organized Humans First, which was bipartisan and now is focusing only on organizing conservatives, was an early founder or organizer with the Tea Party way back when. And this has a similar vibe to me. It’s not a left-right thing. It’s a populous technocrat divide.You’re seeing that on the right and the left. So for example, at the Abundance Conference last year, it was center-right to center-left-ish. And everybody was pro-nuclear, pro-AI. And we were hearing that, “These things are here to stay. We have to figure out how to do it smartly.” At the same time, the populist left and the populist right are both skeptical of tech development, to put it lightly.That skepticism plays out across a number of dimensions. I couldn’t help but be struck as I read your story by how many strains of conspiracy thinking there are about data centers.I’m curious if they’re just visible. They’re so big, and they require so much development and so much build-out that you can just glue any concerns you have onto them. “This big thing is happening, and I don’t feel any control. And I’m also worried about 5G, Chinese government interference, and X, Y, Z. And I can just point it all at this very big thing by which there’s a process to say no. I can go to my local town board meeting and literally say no.”I mean, I think that’s part of it. It’s interesting because I think there’s a spectrum of conspiratorial thinking to, I guess, misinformed thinking on the water use question. We now know that they don’t use as much water as we previously thought, et cetera, et cetera. But on the far end of the spectrum, one of the people I talked to told me that cattle born near data centers are all stillborn. I tried to track that down. I was like, “Where did this come from?” And it was one farmer in Texas who claims he had one stillborn calf on his cattle farm.So that got spun out via the internet rumor, social media mill. I think that’s part of it. There’s this issue of social collapse that comes out once you talk to people a little bit. One of the women I talked to said, “I had this friend. ChatGPT told her she couldn’t be friends with me anymore.” You have all of these stories of people harming themselves, going off their medication, or whatever because they’ve been talking to a chatbot and it goes awry.I think this gives people a feeling of control. Where I can go to my community board meeting or my council members’ meeting, and I can say, “I don’t want this big building that houses the scary thing that is fracturing my community here.” So it’s not just the actual building. I think it’s a broader backlash to generative AI and to LLMs specifically.One of my ideas that I’ve been pushing on lately is that the AI products are not winning over hearts and minds in the market. So if the data centers just said Netflix on them, maybe people would like them more.But instead, that’s where the slop is coming from, and it’s why the jobs are going to go away. It’s also where Mark Zuckerberg is just going to get even wealthier. Is there a dynamic of that — that people just don’t like the thing that the data centers make?Yes, absolutely. They don’t like a lot of the things that the data centers make. It’s not just AI. I think AI is a big part of it, but this is a little preview of a different story I’m working on... In Tucson, there’s a data center project that’s getting built out. The people I talked to there said, “Yeah, this might be an Amazon Web Services facility, and Amazon works with ICE.” So this technology is fueling mass deportations through, not directly, but creating the non-sexy infrastructure that surveillance is built on.There are two things to it. Part of it is a NIMBY, “I don’t want this thing in my backyard, literally. I don’t want my town to get polluted. I don’t want this. I don’t want that. I don’t want to see it. I don’t want the noise pollution.” And then the other part is, “I do not like what this big building represents and what it has wrought on society.”Does that cut across bipartisan lines? Or is that more culture war coded?It’s both. It cuts across culture war lines in that people have different concerns about what LLMs do. So one woman I spoke to was talking about the fracturing of social bonds. On the construction front, she was like, “We’re a rural-ish community. We don’t want this big blight on our nice rolling hills.” So that’s a right-coded thing. And there was a lot of anti-development stuff that is neither right nor left.On the left, I would say there’s similar culture war concerns, but it’s... I don’t know if this is necessarily a culture war concern, but fueling deportations. Both sides, I think, are concerned about the job losses because of AI. And both sides have caught on to the fact that these facilities don’t really have a lot of long-term job prospects. There’s the big construction boom. There’s an HVAC situation. But to actually maintain these facilities, it doesn’t require that many people.I think people have caught onto that. The promises of the AI data job, or that the AI boom will lead to jobs related to data centers, are not actually true.Yeah. At most, it’s a few hundred jobs for each of these facilities, at least in the data centers we have now. Why do you think some of the protests make national news? The Kevin O’Leary data center in Utah is a national story. Maybe it’s just because he’s a cartoon character.And then there’s a new project in Georgia where there might be a huge OpenAI facility that seems to go under the radar. There are all of the projects in Florida that you are reporting on, but don’t seem to be explosive in the way that some of the other ones are.Yeah, I think that’s a good question. There was one in Florida that was explosive, and it was just because it was near Mar-a-Lago. I think that one pretty obviously made the national news because it’s related to the president. I honestly think a cartoon character at the center of it is the deciding factor a lot of the time on whether it’ll become a national story or not. And then also the numbers. The Utah one, I don’t remember off the top of my head how big it’s supposed to be, but it’s supposed to be huge. So then that becomes a proxy for all data center development.They’re being planned everywhere. And I think what’s so interesting is that the backlash exists everywhere too. I relied a lot on, for example, the Tampa Bay Times to figure out the background for this story. They’re on top of it. They’re going to these meetings and watching people get yelled at and asked, “Did you sign an NDA? Yes or no?“Do you think the local governments are being responsive? You’ve now gone to some of these protests; you’ve talked to people on the ground in various counties across the country. The basic unit of democracy is supposed to be your local government because you know those people and you can yell at them in the grocery store and the town board meeting. We’re seeing there’s a wall going up in some of these cases where the local governments are saying, “No, we have to do this development. This is the only economic development available.” And the people are saying, “No, we’re going to throw you out.” Do you think local governments on the whole are being responsive or not responsive at all?I think it really depends. In Hernando County, they did pass a moratorium. There are a lot of counties in Florida where moratoriums have passed. But in Tucson, again, the city government is responsive to what the people want and the county government isn’t, and they’re at odds with each other. There are all these videos of people yelling at their representatives about NDAs again. And then them being like, “We cannot say whether we signed an NDA,” which is an answer, but whatever.I think it really depends on a lot of things. How small the communities are, for one. How vulnerable the people in office feel to getting voted out, I think, is another big one. In Florida, the Republican primary for governor, I think, might be affected by this issue. The primary is in a few weeks and the front-runner, Byron Donalds, has taken a lot of money from the AI industry and data center development groups. And people are mad. People are really mad.He was endorsed by Trump, and everyone I spoke to, as proud Trump voters, said things like, “I don’t understand why Trump would endorse him. I’m not going to vote for him.” One woman I talked to who told me she was opposed to everything Democrat said she would vote for a Democrat or an independent if Donalds won the primary. And Donalds has also changed… not his stance on data center development, but the way that he talks about it in response to a lot of this backlash.How has he changed the stance? How is he talking about it now?He says his vision is to make Florida the financial capital of the world. And to a lot of people, that would sound great, but these people are really upset by this, both because they... I mean, there are a lot of other things at play here. Housing costs in Florida have gone up exponentially. Not only in big cities like Miami, but in the suburbs of Tampa, for example. Housing prices have shot up to levels that I, as somebody who grew up there, just don’t understand. I literally can’t wrap my head around it.So I think a lot of the backlash to development and to data centers is also related to people’s cost of living going up and to these, in their words, outside developers coming in and changing a community that’s already changing. He has since said that we need data center development, but we need to do it responsibly.Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is another great example of this. He supported a bill that would require data centers to pay their own utilities and also let counties require them to use reclaimed water, which would address the water issue. But the Tampa Bay Times reported that he also supported legislation that gives massive tax breaks to data centers. And that he pushed to amend that law, which I think was signed in 2017, to only apply to hyperscale data centers, which are the ones that people have problems with.The people I talk to, they know that there are currently data centers in Florida, and they’re smaller. There are no hyperscale data centers, but there are around one hundred smaller ones for Netflix or whatever. And they’re okay with that. One woman I talked to works in IT. She said, “I understand that data centers are a boogeyman, and we need them for stuff. But I don’t want this massive facility using all of our power, emitting these frequencies, et cetera, et cetera.” Another thing that I think is really interesting-Wait, can you just explain what “emitting these frequencies” means?[Laughs] Just the noise. I talked to these guys at the Border Security Expo who work for a data center company, and they all live in Virginia. Even they were like, “Yeah, it sucks.” They said, “I hate walking around my neighborhood because I just hear it all the time.” And they work in data centers. I don’t think she meant 5G.It’s a real element of this, right next to China being a villain of whatever persuasion you need China to be a villain for. Again, there’s just a piece of all this where it’s a big thing that you can stop. The power of NIMBYism can stop this. Maybe we can’t stop everything else. We can’t stop Facebook from doing targeted advertising that feels like it’s listening to you. No one knows how to stop this. It’s bad. We don’t like it, but no one knows how to stop it.“I can stop this building from being built” seems like it not only scrambles our culture war lines, but it’s scrambling politics, too. Byron Donalds saying he wants Florida to be the financial capital of the world. One, it’s very funny in that he has to contend with the existence of New York, London, Beijing, and Amsterdam. Go down the line. There are a lot of places that can compete for that title where Miami might not be in the running. But doing it via building data centers is not the path to that result. It’s just a bunch of economic development that might result in some short-term gains.It feels like people have clocked it, and they’ve clocked that it’s a thing you can stop. I’m curious if there’s anything else. You’ve spent a lot of time covering the right, and I wonder if there’s anything else that scrambles the lines like that. Because in almost every other case, “let’s build stuff, let’s tear down the White House and build a ballroom” is fine. Building things is better, and it is coded in one side of the culture war.Yeah. I mean, this is, again, so Florida specific, but it really surprised me how much of the politics around this were scrambled. One of the women was talking about this ballot initiative that’s going to pass. It’s going to give more tax exemptions to homeowners, which I feel is a standard Republican thing — lower taxes for homeowners. People would like that.She said, “This is terrible. It’s going to deprive county governments of funds that they would otherwise get from homeowners, which will then entice the counties even further to have data centers come into our communities.” So she was thinking of the second- and third-order effects of this, even though that’s a pretty populist initiative. But yeah, it’s all so scrambled.How do you see the scramble inside of the right and then carrying over to the populist left? The idea that a bunch of billionaires threw all of their weight behind Donald Trump in 2024, and that led to, I don’t know, a bunch of podcast bros throwing their weight behind Donald Trump in 2024. There was a cultural wave of Peter Thiel, Marc Andreessen, Elon Musk, and the All-In podcast about building and tech and the future. It feels like that has come to one kind of end.I don’t think that that wave is driving the culture anymore because of the backlash to AI. We can all see the college students booing at graduation. If the backlash is there against the data centers, against AI taking the jobs, against billionaires in general, what does that turn into on the right? Because that was the animating force of the right for so long.I think that is still an open question. I think the question is whether this backlash is strong enough to shake people’s other partisan concerns.If you’ve got a Democrat candidate who is anti-data center development, but also not super gung-ho about deputizing all Florida police officers to do ICE arrests, where does that leave someone who supports Trump’s immigration policies but doesn’t want a data center in their neighborhood? I don’t know. I think that’s what the party is struggling with right now.I mean, I think Trump is this perfect avatar for people because he somehow stands for anti-elite sentiment, but also for hard work and capitalism. He’s just this perfect blend of, I don’t even know how to describe it. He contains multitudes, I guess. And nobody else can contain multitudes like him. They don’t have the juice. They just don’t have it.Can I make the argument?Yeah.I think I can make the argument. I grew up in Wisconsin, which has many similar dynamics to maybe Florida, in that people in Wisconsin remember a time when there were big factories. In the town I grew up in, Racine, there used to be a Case factory that made tractors. There was a Chrysler factory in Kenosha that made Jeep Wranglers. This is a real thing that occurred, and all those things are gone. So Trump would promise all of this huge economic development that basically looked like manufacturing. I think what his version of this, even with tariffs, was, “We will bring manufacturing back to all of these places. And that manufacturing will require a lot of hard work, but there will be dignity in that hard work.”At the end of it, you’re going to get to point to a Modine air conditioner and be like, “I made that thing. My community made that thing.” I think that is very seductive. I mean, Trump spent years promising that we would build iPhones in America, and that’s Wisconsin and Foxconn and all this stuff.Maybe none of those things were ever going to come true because that’s not how anything gets made anymore. And that’s not even the kind of work people actually want to do in America anymore. But you take all of that energy, and you’re like, “Actually, what we’re going to make is data centers.” And no one can see at the end of that, “I made a Jeep Wrangler.” They get to see that Elon Musk got richer; they just lost their jobs, their children feel like they have no future, and their feeds are full of slop.And I feel like something gets disconnected in the multitudes where you can tell everyone, “Yeah, the best I can do for you is make you the world’s richest factory foreman.” So people are like, “That sounds awesome. That’s better than whatever nonsense I’m doing online.” But you can’t be like, “I’m going to make Sam Altman richer,” because that doesn’t mean anything to anyone. All of this construction doesn’t do anything for anyone.I look at the backlash, and all I see is that a lot of people across the political spectrum have come to that realization. You can tear down our communities to build bridges and factories, and you can pollute the skies with smokestacks as long as we all get jobs. But if you’re going to do all that and all I get is more AI-generated movie posters on Amazon Prime whose price keeps going up every month, screw you. And I’m wondering if that connection is... That’s my guess. I’m wondering if you see any hints of that connection in your reporting as you talk to all these people.I think so. I think the Florida version of making a Jeep Wrangler is like, there were orange groves and cattle ranches, and now there are not. I used to drive past an orange grove when I was a kid. That orange grove is gone. It’s a Publix now. There was an old cow field. Now that’s a mall.On the one hand, that’s what people want. People want consumption, but they also, at least in Florida, liked thinking that they lived near an orange grove. Like, “Oh, maybe the guy’s using tons of pesticides. Maybe the orange grove is worse for your health than the data center.” I don’t know. I don’t have the stats on this. But you could see the tangible effects of what your economy was producing.Now it’s just like, “There’s a building that none of us can go in. It makes a horrible noise. And I think it’s drinking all my water?” And then it’s also making your kids dumb and alienated, and making everybody lose their jobs. People don’t like that.Again, these aren’t Luddites. The woman I talked to said, “I found out about the Humans First organizing [efforts] via Facebook. I know there’s an irony in that. I know there’s an irony in me working in IT and opposing this data center.” They’re not dumb. They understand that all of these things that we’ve built our lives around require something to power them. They just don’t want that something to be within driving distance of their house. They want it somewhere else.And it’s unclear where that somewhere else should be apart from space.Apart from space.That is a very different episode of Decoder. But that’s one answer the industry has: “These people, their stupid concerns are too annoying. We’ll just put the data centers in space,” and maybe they’ll solve that problem. Who knows?The other answer is, “We’ll just horsepower over their concerns. This is too important. We’re going to do it anyway. And maybe we’ll just subsidize a bunch of education in some community. Maybe we’ll just pay a bunch of extra money. Maybe we’ll pay for everyone’s electricity.”I don’t know if those have gotten any traction. Is there anything that the tech companies or the neoclouds could do in these communities to overcome the objections? Could they just pay for healthcare? Or is that just a non-starter?I don’t know about paying for healthcare, but something that I didn’t include in the piece, because it was extremely dry and very technical, was that the small protest ended with about an hour and a half long presentation from a land use expert on how to write local zoning ordinances to prevent hyperscale data centers from being built. It was really specific stuff, like “You could have them on multiple small parcels of land.” It was really dry. “You could require them to use this amount of reclaimed water, et cetera, et cetera.”I think what people want more than the data centers not being there is a degree of community input on how they’re built — if they’re going to be built. I think if they got that, they would maybe not be pacified, but they would at least not feel like there’s a big external force coming in and steamrolling their community, especially when they already feel like that in every other aspect of their life.This is the thing that I’m most curious about. So much of our politics and our culture has been nationalized. Everything happens at the national level. The fact that the mayor of New York is a national political figure is at once very silly and also just the funniest thing that has happened in a long time.Data centers are very local. They’re happening to people in their backyards, and a data center being built in Florida, Georgia, or Tucson has nothing to do with me in New York. It’s far away enough.Maybe what you’re hearing from everybody is just, “Somewhere else, and as we get to somewhere else, I won’t care.” But it is very local. And then it is very in person. People are going to the meetings; they’re encountering one another. There have been stories of bridges across party lines from people who would never like each other normally because they both hate the data centers.Is there an element of a return to actual local politics and actual community building here that could be catalyzed by opposition to data centers?I really think so. Again, I’m talking to organizers in multiple states who are going to these community, town council, or county council meetings and yelling at their representatives. And sometimes it’s hundreds of people. I think this is maybe a weird analogy, but it reminds me of the local backlash to right-wing organizing and local education policy, which is where a lot of the anti-trans backlash started. You’d go into the school board, and you’d be like, “I don’t want this gender stuff being taught to my child. I don’t want my kids to know that slavery was bad.”I’m not comparing them in terms of value judgment. I just think it’s at a level of local engagement that is at the same time a national issue. It’s these really, really, really localized policies that may end up driving, if not national policy change and national policy discussions, but at least national political vibes. Whoever wins the Democratic and Republican primaries and runs for president in 2028, what are they going to be saying about data centers? I don’t know, but I know it’s going to be informed by what happens this year and next year.I’m actually very curious how Trump handles it. As you said, he contains multitudes. He’s very good at reading his own base. It feels like the Trump base is very much polarized around data centers. There are a lot of people who love Donald Trump but hate data centers. And then there’s his money, which loves the AI build-out and loves data centers. That is a fracture as deep as anything.A lot of those folks will say, “AI just has a marketing problem. If only we could convince people of the benefits of this build-out and the super intelligence to come, they would be on board.”The best marketer they could have for that would be Donald Trump. But he doesn’t seem to be willing to make those claims at the level that they might need. And certainly he is very attuned to his base hating AI. How do you think he’s going to play it? And how do you think the MAGA coalition will respond to it?Okay, so do you remember when Trump was talking about H-1B visas? Or not even when he was talking about it, but just the whole swirl around what we’re going to do about these?Yeah.Trump said, “I think we should stamp an H-1B visa to every foreign student’s college graduation diploma.” And I thought, “What are you talking about? Your administration is charging $100,000 for these visas.” He kept saying things like, “These kids are really smart. We need them in America building chips.”I think he’s just going to do it like that. The thing about Trump is that he can say literally whatever, and he can do literally whatever, and the people who like him will continue to like him. Sometimes they’ll be like, “Oh, well, I don’t like this particular policy of his. I don’t know why he endorsed this candidate,” but they’re still going to back the guy.But enough to split the difference on this issue? In every other issue, he could polarize the electorate, and he would get there, but, “I’m going to put a data center in the backyard, and it’s going to make that noise.” Maybe not enough.But the thing is that they don’t see it as coming from Trump. They’re thinking, “These companies are coming into our community.” And if you connect the dots, it’s like, “Who supports those companies? The president. Who is giving the president a lot of money? All these different companies.”That’s not how people see it. They see it as these tech oligarchs who are just disconnected from politics and disconnected from anything because of all their money. They don’t see that as having a connection to the president. Instead, they see that as having a connection to the governor, to the board of commissioners, or whatever. But Trump is floating above it all. I don’t know why.Well, I’m curious, and maybe we should end it here. The Florida gubernatorial primaries are coming up. If Donalds loses, even with that Trump endorsement over the data center issue, do you think that will be a signal or a predictor of what will happen in the midterms?I think it would be a massive signal, if only because Donalds is polling so much further ahead than everybody else. He’s the clear frontrunner, and the lieutenant governor who’s polling second is also pro-data centers. If any of the anti-data center candidates win the Republican primary, that is going to be huge and completely unexpected by everybody in the state. But it could happen. Crazier things have happened.We’re going to be doing a lot of coverage of this in the months to come, especially ahead of the midterms, because this scrambling of party lines, this scrambling of the culture war, seems very important. The politics we’ve had for so long, they don’t seem like they can hold up to everyone hating the same thing.Maybe that’s all America needs. It does seem like every American hating these big buildings that make loud noises might be the thing that unifies us, which is good or bad. You can make your own decisions, but I can’t think of anything else. There’s nothing else that’s cutting across party lines this way. Can you?Literally nothing. Nothing at all. And it’s cutting across party lines, I think, not just in that people hate it, but I had these deeply conservative women talking to me about local environmental and ecological issues. They were talking about pesticides and forever chemicals in their water, which you wouldn’t expect looking at Republican politics five to 10 years ago, that this is where we have ended up.We’re still doing climate change hoaxes at the national level, and on the ground we’re talking about pesticides. There’s something there.Gaby, we’re going to have to have you back as the story develops and certainly as we go into all these elections. Thank you so much for being at Decoder.Yeah, thanks for having me. This was fun.Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!Decoder with Nilay PatelA podcast from The Verge about big ideas and other problems.SUBSCRIBE NOW!Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.Nilay Patel

content_html_zh:
今天，我正在与 The Verge 的政策记者 Gaby Del Valle 谈论针对人工智能数据中心日益增长的抵制情绪。

盖比最近报道了一篇关于佛罗里达州埃尔南多县的精彩文章，该县委员会上个月一致批准暂停数据中心建设一年。 她参加了一个名为“人类优先”的组织组织的抗议活动，这是一个专注于打击人工智能数据中心扩建的保守草根运动。

Verge 订阅者，不要忘记，无论您在何处获取播客，都可以获得无广告解码器的独占访问权限。 前往这里。 还不是订阅者？ 您可以在这里注册。

你会听到盖比解释说，这是两党更大规模、更广泛的反对数据中心的一部分。 不仅作为实体建筑，而且作为基础设施，为人工智能的繁荣提供动力，夺走当地的就业机会并用污水填充饲料。

数据中心建设已经成为公众对人工智能感受的代表：他们可以将恐惧和沮丧的情绪集中在有形的东西上，甚至可以通过社区组织和抗议产生足够的压力来阻止。

因此，我想让盖比向我讲述这些抗议活动的实际情况，这些抗议活动来自那些政党背景通常与大企业结盟的选民。 你会听到盖比说数据中心正在扰乱政党界限，将顽固的特朗普选民变成了关心地下水污染和永久化学品等左派问题的抗议者。

这是一个令人困惑的时期，数据中心将在未来的选举政治中发挥重要作用。 所以我怀疑这不会是我们最后一次听到盖比关于“人类优先”等运动的消息。

好的：Verge 政策记者 Gaby Del Valle 谈论两党数据中心的强烈反对。 开始了。

为了篇幅和清晰度，本次采访经过了轻微编辑。

Gaby Del Valle，您是 The Verge 的政策记者。 欢迎回到解码器。

谢谢。 很高兴来到这里。

我很高兴能和你说话。 您之前曾与我们的朋友 Alex Heath 一起上过节目，但这是我第一次在 Decoder 中与您交谈。 我认为你刚刚写的关于佛罗里达州数据中心和保守派强烈反对的故事只是中期选举中科技政策的真实预览。

你就在那里。 您与一群抗议数据中心的人进行了交谈。 就我们的政治而言，这是一场真正的结盟争夺战。 告诉我们你发现了什么。

我发现人们真的、真的、真的、真的很生气。 他们生气的原因因社区而异，但如果有道理的话，他们也是一样的。 他们有局部的担忧。 他们告诉我佛罗里达真的很潮湿。 在如此潮湿的地方建造一个需要保持非常凉爽和干燥的数据中心是没有意义的。 他们中的许多人担心地下水。 他们担心 PFAS 会被倾倒到水中。

但我也与亚利桑那州的人们交谈过，他们有相反的担忧。 亚利桑那州不是很潮湿。 亚利桑那州非常干燥。 他们还说，“在沙漠中建立数据中心没有意义。” 因此，无论您的社区是什么，您都会想，“由于某些原因，在这里建立数据中心是没有意义的”。

在阅读您的文章并听到您为即将发表的文章所做的其他报道时，真正令我震惊的是，数据中心的扩建和数据中心的抗议活动并没有完全符合我们长期以来所看到的通常的左右文化战争联盟。 我很好奇你对此的看法。 为什么埃隆·马斯克不能命令他的追随者大军支持数据中心呢？

这对我来说很有趣。 这是一些背景故事，可以回答您的问题。 组织“人类优先”组织的女性是两党合作组织，现在只专注于组织保守派，她是茶党的早期创始人或组织者。 这和我有相似的感觉。 这不是左右的事情。 这是人口众多的技术官僚分歧。

你会在右边和左边看到它。 例如，在去年的丰盛会议上，它是从中右到中左的。 每个人都支持核能、支持人工智能。 我们听到这样的话：“这些东西会一直存在。 我们必须弄清楚如何巧妙地做到这一点。” 与此同时，民粹主义左翼和民粹主义右翼都对科技发展持怀疑态度。

这种怀疑体现在多个​​方面。 当我读到你的故事时，我不禁被关于数据中心的阴谋思想之多所震惊。

我很好奇它们是否只是可见的。 它们太大了，需要太多的开发和扩建，你可以把任何担忧都粘在它们身上。 “这件大事正在发生，我感觉不到任何控制。 我还担心 5G、中国政府的干预以及 X、Y、Z。 我可以把这一切都指向这个非常大的事情，通过这个过程可以说不。 我可以去参加当地的城镇董事会会议并直接说不。”

我的意思是，我认为这是其中的一部分。 这很有趣，因为我认为存在一系列阴谋思维，我猜，对用水问题的误导性思维。 我们现在知道他们使用的水并不像我们之前想象的那么多，等等。 但在极端情况下，一位与我交谈过的人告诉我，在数据中心附近出生的牛都是死产。 我试图追踪它。 我当时想，“这是从哪里来的？” 德克萨斯州的一位农民声称他的养牛场有一头死产的小牛。

这就是通过互联网谣言、社交媒体工厂流传出来的。 我认为这是其中的一部分。 一旦你和人们稍微交谈一下，就会出现社会崩溃的问题。 我采访过的一位女士说：“我有一个朋友。 ChatGPT 告诉她她不能再和我做朋友了。” 你有很多这样的故事：人们伤害自己，停止服药，或者其他什么，因为他们一直在与聊天机器人交谈，但结果出了问题。

我认为这给人一种掌控感。 我可以在那里参加社区委员会会议或理事会成员会议，我可以说：“我不想要这座大楼，里面有可怕的东西，它正在破坏我的社区。” 所以这不仅仅是实际的建筑。 我认为这是对生成式人工智能，特别是法学硕士的更广泛的抵制。

我最近一直在推行的想法之一是，人工智能产品并没有赢得市场的青睐。 因此，如果数据中心只在上面标明 Netflix，也许人们会更喜欢它们。

但相反，这就是污水的来源，也是工作机会消失的原因。 这也是马克·扎克伯格变得更加富有的地方。 是否存在这样一种动态——人们就是不喜欢数据中心制造的东西？

是的，绝对是。 他们不喜欢数据中心制造的很多东西。 这不仅仅是人工智能。 我认为人工智能是其中的重要组成部分，但这是我正在研究的另一个故事的一个小预览…… 在图森，有一个数据中心项目正在建设中。 与我交谈过的人说：“是的，这可能是亚马逊网络服务设施，亚马逊与 ICE 合作。” 因此，这项技术不是直接推动大规模驱逐出境，而是通过创建监视所依赖的非性感基础设施。

有两件事。 其中一部分是邻避，“从字面上看，我不想让这个东西出现在我的后院。 我不想让我的小镇被污染。 我不想要这个。 我不想那样。 我不想看到它。 我不想要噪音污染。” 另一部分是，“我不喜欢这座大楼所代表的意义以及它对社会造成的影响。”

这是否跨越了两党的界限？ 还是更多的文化战争编码？

两者都是。 它跨越了文化战线，因为人们对法学硕士的工作有不同的担忧。 我采访过的一位女士正在谈论社会纽带的破裂。 在建设方面，她说，“我们是一个农村社区。 我们不希望我们美丽的连绵起伏的山丘受到如此大的破坏。” 所以这是一个正确编码的事情。 还有很多反发展的东西，既不右也不左。

在左边，我想说也有类似的文化战争担忧，但它...... 我不知道这是否一定是文化战争问题，但却加剧了驱逐。 我认为双方都担心人工智能导致的失业问题。 双方都认识到这样一个事实：这些设施实际上并没有太多的长期就业前景。 这里有巨大的建筑热潮。 有暖通空调的情况。 但要真正维护这些设施，并不需要那么多人。

我认为人们已经意识到了这一点。 人工智能数据工作的承诺，或者人工智能的繁荣将带来与数据中心相关的工作，实际上并不真实。

是的。 每个设施最多只能提供数百​​个工作岗位，至少在我们现在拥有的数据中心是这样。 您认为为什么一些抗议活动会成为全国新闻？ 犹他州的凯文·奥利里数据中心是一个全国性的故事。 也许只是因为他是一个卡通人物。

然后佐治亚州有一个新项目，那里可能有一个巨大的 OpenAI 设施，但似乎没有受到关注。 您正在报道佛罗里达州的所有项目，但似乎不像其他一些项目那样具有爆炸性。

是的，我认为这是一个好问题。 佛罗里达州有一个爆炸性事件，只是因为它靠近海湖庄园。 我认为这件事显然成为了全国新闻，因为它与总统有关。 老实说，我认为它的中心卡通人物很多时候是它是否会成为全国性故事的决定因素。 然后还有数字。 犹他州的，我不记得它应该有多大，但它应该很大。 那么这就成为所有数据中心发展的代表。

各地都在计划着它们。 我认为有趣的是，这种强烈反对也无处不在。 例如，我非常依赖坦帕湾时报来了解这个故事的背景。 他们在上面。 他们去参加这些会议，看着人们被吼叫并被问：“你签署了保密协议吗？ 是还是不是？”

您认为当地政府的反应是否积极？ 你现在已经参加了其中一些抗议活动；您已经与全国各个县的实地人员进行了交谈。 民主的基本单位应该是当地政府，因为你认识那些人，你可以在杂货店和镇议会会议上对他们大喊大叫。

我们看到，在某些情况下，地方政府会说：“不，我们必须进行这项开发。 这是唯一可用的经济发展。” 人们说：“不，我们要把你赶出去。” 您认为地方政府总体上是积极响应还是根本不响应？

我认为这确实取决于。 在埃尔南多县，他们确实通过了一项暂停令。 佛罗里达州有很多县已经通过了暂停令。 但在图森，市政府对人民的需求做出了回应，而县政府却没有，而且他们之间存在分歧。 所有这些视频都显示人们再次就保密协议向他们的代表大喊大叫。 然后他们说，“我们不能说我们是否签署了保密协议”，这是一个答案，但无论如何。

我认为这确实取决于很多事情。 其一，社区有多小。 我认为，办公室里的人对被投票下台感到多么脆弱是另一个大问题。 我认为，在佛罗里达州，共和党州长初选可能会受到这个问题的影响。 初选将在几周后举行，领先者拜伦·唐纳德 (Byron Donalds) 从人工智能行业和数据中心开发团队那里获得了大量资金。 人们很生气。 人们真的很生气。

他得到了特朗普的支持，与我交谈过的每个人，作为自豪的特朗普选民，都说：“我不明白为什么特朗普会支持他。 我不会投票给他。” 我采访过的一位女士告诉我，她反对民主党所说的一切，如果唐纳德赢得初选，她将投票给民主党或独立人士。 唐纳德也变了…… 不是他对数据中心发展的立场，而是他针对这种强烈反对而谈论数据中心的方式。

他如何改变立场？ 他现在怎么谈论这件事了？

他说他的愿景是让佛罗里达成为世界金融之都。 对于很多人来说，这听起来很棒，但这些人真的对此感到不安，因为他们...... 我的意思是，这里还有很多其他事情在起作用。 佛罗里达州的住房成本呈指数级上涨。 不仅在迈阿密这样的大城市，而且在坦帕的郊区也是如此。 房价已飙升至我作为在那里长大的人无法理解的水平。 我真的无法理解它。

因此，我认为对开发和数据中心的强烈反对也与人们生活成本的上升有关，用他们的话说，与外部开发人员的进来并改变了已经发生变化的社区有关。 他此后表示，我们需要数据中心的发展，但我们需要负责任地这样做。

佛罗里达州州长 罗恩·德桑蒂斯是另一个很好的例子。 他支持一项法案，要求数据中心支付自己的水电费，并让各县要求它们使用再生水，这将解决水问题。 但《坦帕湾时报》报道称，他还支持为数据中心提供大规模税收减免的立法。 他推动修改了这项法律（我认为该法律是在 2017 年签署的），使其仅适用于超大规模数据中心，而人们对这些数据中心存在疑问。

与我交谈的人知道，佛罗里达州目前有数据中心，而且规模较小。 没有超大规模的数据中心，但有大约一百个较小的数据中心供 Netflix 或其他公司使用。 他们对此表示同意。 我采访过一位从事 IT 工作的女性。 她说：“我知道数据中心是一个恶魔，我们需要它们来做东西。 但我不希望这个巨大的设施使用我们所有的电力，发射这些频率，等等。” 还有一件事我觉得很有趣——

等等，你能解释一下“发射这些频率”是什么意思吗？

[笑]只是噪音。 我在边境安全博览会上与这些在一家数据中心公司工作的人进行了交谈，他们都住在弗吉尼亚州。 就连他们也说：“是的，这很糟糕。” 他们说：“我讨厌在附近走动，因为我总是听到这种声音。” 他们在数据中心工作。 我不认为她指的是5G。

这是其中的一个真正因素，就在中国成为恶棍之后，无论你需要中国成为恶棍的说服力是什么。 再说一次，这一切中只有一小部分是你可以阻止的大事。 邻避主义的力量可以阻止这一切。 也许我们无法阻止其他一切。 我们无法阻止 Facebook 做有针对性的广告，让人感觉它在倾听你的声音。 没有人知道如何阻止这一切。 这很糟糕。 我们不喜欢它，但没有人知道如何阻止它。

“我可以阻止这座建筑的建造”似乎不仅扰乱了我们的文化战线，而且也扰乱了政治。 拜伦·唐纳德斯 (Byron Donalds) 表示，他希望佛罗里达州成为世界金融之都。 第一，非常有趣的是，他必须应对纽约、伦敦、北京和阿姆斯特丹的存在。 往下走吧。

有很多地方可以争夺这个冠军，但迈阿密可能不在其中。 但通过建设数据中心来实现这一目标并不是实现这一结果的途径。 这只是一系列可能带来一些短期收益的经济发展。

感觉就像人们已经记录了它，并且他们记录了这是一件你可以阻止的事情。 我很好奇是否还有其他事情。 你花了很多时间覆盖右边，我想知道是否还有其他东西会像这样打乱线路。 因为在几乎所有其他情况下，“让我们建造一些东西，让我们拆掉白宫并建造一个舞厅”就可以了。 建造东西更好，它是在文化战争的一方面编码的。

是的。 我的意思是，这又是佛罗里达州特有的，但令我惊讶的是，围绕这件事的政治有多少是混乱的。 其中一位女性正在谈论这项即将通过的投票倡议。 它将给予房主更多的免税，我认为这是共和党的标准做法——降低房主的税收。 人们会喜欢这样的。

她说：“这太可怕了。 这将剥夺县政府原本可以从房主那里获得的资金，从而进一步吸引县政府将数据中心引入我们的社区。” 因此，她正在考虑这样做的二阶和三阶效应，尽管这是一项相当民粹主义的举措。 但是，是的，一切都那么混乱。

您如何看待右翼内部的争夺，然后蔓延到民粹主义左翼？ 一群亿万富翁在 2024 年全力支持唐纳德·特朗普的想法，我不知道，这导致了一群播客兄弟在 2024 年全力支持唐纳德·特朗普。 彼得·泰尔 (Peter Thiel)、马克·安德森 (Marc Andreessen)、埃隆·马斯克 (Elon Musk) 以及有关建筑、科技和未来的 All-In 播客掀起了一股文化浪潮。 感觉好像已经到了某种结局。

由于对人工智能的强烈反对，我认为这种浪潮不再推动文化。 我们都可以看到大学生在毕业时发出嘘声。 如果反对数据中心、反对人工智能抢走工作、反对亿万富翁，那么右翼会变成什么样子？ 因为长期以来，这就是右翼的活力力量。

我认为这仍然是一个悬而未决的问题。 我认为问题在于这种强烈反对是否足以动摇人们对其他党派的担忧。

如果你有一位反对数据中心开发的民主党候选人，但也不太热衷于代表所有佛罗里达州警察执行 ICE 逮捕行动，那么支持特朗普移民政策但不希望在他们的社区建立数据中心的人会怎样呢？ 我不知道。 我认为这就是该党目前正在努力解决的问题。

我的意思是，我认为特朗普是人们的完美化身，因为他在某种程度上代表了反精英情绪，但也代表了努力工作和资本主义。 他就是这种完美的融合，我什至不知道如何描述它。 我猜他包含了很多人。 没有人能像他一样容纳这么多人。 他们没有果汁。 他们只是没有。

我可以提出论据吗？

Yeah.

我想我可以提出论点。 我在威斯康星州长大，那里的动态可能与佛罗里达有很多相似之处，因为威斯康星州的人们记得曾经有大工厂。 在我长大的小镇拉辛，曾经有一家生产拖拉机的凯斯工厂。 基诺沙有一家克莱斯勒工厂，生产吉普牧马人。 这是真实发生过的事情，那些事情都已经过去了。

因此，特朗普会承诺所有这些基本上看起来像制造业的巨大经济发展。 我认为，即使有关税，他的版本是：“我们将把制造业带回所有这些地方。 制造业需要大量的艰苦工作，但艰苦工作中会有尊严。”

最后，你会指着一台 Modine 空调说：“那东西是我做的。 我的社区创造了那件事。” 我认为这非常诱人。 我的意思是，特朗普花了数年时间承诺我们将在美国生产 iPhone，那就是威斯康星州和富士康以及所有这些东西。

也许这些事情都不会实现，因为这不再是任何东西的制造方式。 这甚至不再是人们在美国真正想做的工作。 但当你吸收了所有的能量后，你会想，“实际上，我们要做的是数据中心。” 没有人能看到最后，“我制造了一辆吉普牧马人。” 他们看到埃隆·马斯克变得更富有；他们刚刚失去了工作，他们的孩子觉得自己没有未来，他们的食物里充满了粪便。

我觉得在人群中有些东西被脱节了，你可以告诉每个人，“是的，我能为你做的最好的事情就是让你成为世界上最富有的工厂工头。” 所以人们会说，“这听起来棒极了。 这比我在网上做的任何废话都要好。” 但你不能说，“我会让萨姆·奥尔特曼变得更富有”，因为这对任何人来说都没有任何意义。 所有这些建设对任何人都没有任何作用。

我观察了人们的强烈反对，我看到的是各个政治派别的很多人都意识到了这一点。 你可以拆除我们的社区来建造桥梁和工厂，只要我们都能找到工作，你就可以用烟囱污染天空。 但如果你打算做这一切，而我得到的只是亚马逊 Prime 上更多人工智能生成的电影海报，而且价格每个月都在上涨，那就滚蛋吧。 我想知道这种联系是否...... 这是我的猜测。 我想知道当你与所有这些人交谈时，你是否在你的报道中看到了这种联系的任何暗示。

我想是的。 我认为制造吉普牧马人的佛罗里达版本就像是，以前有橘子园和牧场，但现在没有了。 当我还是个孩子的时候，我常常开车经过一片橘子林。 那片橘子林已经消失了。 现在是一个 Publix。 那里有一片古老的牛场。 现在那是一个购物中心。

一方面，这就是人们想要的。 人们想要消费，但他们也喜欢认为自己住在橘子林附近，至少在佛罗里达州是这样。 就像，“哦，也许这家伙使用了大量的杀虫剂。 也许橘子林对你的健康比数据中心更糟糕。” 我不知道。 我没有这方面的统计数据。 但你可以看到你的经济所产生的实际影响。

现在就像是，“有一栋我们谁都不能进去的建筑物。 它发出可怕的噪音。 我想它喝完了我所有的水？” 然后它也会让你的孩子变得愚蠢和疏远，让每个人都失去工作。 人们不喜欢那样。

再说一遍，这些人不是勒德分子。 与我交谈的那位女士说：“我通过 Facebook 了解到人类优先组织[努力]。 我知道这很讽刺。 我知道我从事 IT 工作并反对这个数据中心是一种讽刺。” 他们并不傻。 他们明白，我们赖以生存的所有这些事物都需要某种东西来为其提供动力。 他们只是不希望那个东西在他们家的车程范围内。 他们想要它在其他地方。

目前还不清楚太空之外的其他地方应该在哪里。

除了空间。

这是《解码器》中非常不同的一集。 但这是业界的一个答案：“这些人，他们愚蠢的担忧太烦人了。 我们只需将数据中心放在太空中，”也许他们就能解决这个问题。 谁知道？

另一个答案是：“我们只会加大力度解决他们的担忧。 这太重要了。 无论如何我们都会这么做。 也许我们会补贴一些社区的大量教育。 也许我们只需多付一大笔钱。 也许我们会为每个人支付电费。”

我不知道这些是否有任何吸引力。 科技公司或 Neoclouds 可以在这些社区做些什么来克服这些反对意见吗？ 他们可以只支付医疗费用吗？ 或者这只是一个不可能的开始？

我不知道如何支付医疗费用，但我没有在这篇文章中包含一些内容，因为它非常枯燥且非常技术性，那就是，这场小型抗议以一位土地使用专家大约一个半小时的长篇演讲结束，内容涉及如何编写当地分区条例以防止建造超大规模数据中心。 这确实是具体的东西，比如“你可以把它们放在多块小土地上。” 真的很干。 “你可以要求他们使用这么多的再生水，等等。”

我认为，除了不存在数据中心之外，人们更想要的是社区对数据中心的建设方式（如果要建设的话）提供一定程度的意见。 我认为如果他们得到了这一点，他们可能不会平静，但他们至少不会觉得有一个巨大的外部力量进来并压垮他们的社区，特别是当他们在生活的其他方面已经有这种感觉时。

这是我最好奇的事情。 我们的政治和文化的大部分内容已经被国有化。 一切都发生在国家层面。 纽约市长是一个全国性的政治人物，这一事实既非常愚蠢，又是很长一段时间以来发生的最有趣的事情。

数据中心非常本地化。 这些事情发生在人们的后院，而在佛罗里达州、佐治亚州或图森市建造的数据中心与纽约的我无关。 已经够远了。

也许你从每个人那里听到的只是，“在其他地方，当我们到达其他地方时，我不在乎。” 但这是非常本地化的。 然后这是非常个人化的。 人们去参加会议；他们正在相遇。 有一些关于跨越党派界限的故事，这些人通常不会喜欢对方，因为他们都讨厌数据中心。

对数据中心的反对是否会促进这里回归实际的地方政治和实际的社区建设？

我真的这么认为。 我再次与多个州的组织者交谈，他们将参加这些社区、镇议会或县议会会议，并对他们的代表大喊大叫。 有时有数百人。 我认为这可能是一个奇怪的类比，但它让我想起了当地对右翼组织和当地教育政策的强烈反对，这也是许多反跨性别者强烈反对的开始。 你会进入学校董事会，你会说，“我不想让我的孩子学到性别的东西。 我不想让我的孩子知道奴隶制是不好的。”

我不是在价值判断方面比较它们。 我只是认为这是地方参与的一个层面，同时也是一个全国性的问题。 正是这些真正、真的、真正的本地化政策最终可能会推动国家政策变化和国家政策讨论，但至少会推动国家政治氛围。 无论谁赢得民主党和共和党初选并竞选 2028 年总统，他们会对数据中心有何看法？ 我不知道，但我知道这将取决于今年和明年发生的事情。

其实我很好奇特朗普是怎么处理的。 正如你所说，他包含了众多的人。 他非常擅长解读自己的基础。 感觉特朗普的基地在数据中心方面非常两极分化。 有很多人喜欢唐纳德·特朗普，但讨厌数据中心。 然后是他的钱，喜欢人工智能的建设和数据中心。 那是一个和任何东西一样深的裂缝。

很多人会说，“人工智能只是存在营销问题。 如果我们能让人们相信这种扩建的好处和即将到来的超级智能，他们就会加入。”

他们可能拥有的最佳营销人员是唐纳德·特朗普。 但他似乎不愿意按照他们可能需要的水平提出这些主张。 当然，他非常适应他讨厌人工智能的基础。 你觉得他会怎么玩？ 您认为 MAGA 联盟将如何应对？

好吧，你还记得特朗普何时谈论 H-1B 签证吗？ 或者甚至当他在谈论这件事时也没有，而是整个围绕着我们将要如何处理这些问题？

Yeah.

特朗普表示，“我认为我们应该在每个外国学生的大学毕业文凭上盖上H-1B签证的印章。” 我想：“你在说什么？ 你们的政府对这些签证收取 10 万美元的费用。” 他一直说：“这些孩子真的很聪明。 我们需要他们在美国制造芯片。”

我想他就会这么做。 特朗普的特点是，他可以说任何话，也可以做任何事，喜欢他的人会继续喜欢他。 有时他们会说，“哦，好吧，我不喜欢他的这个特殊政策。 我不知道他为什么支持这位候选人，”但他们仍然会支持这个人。

但足以在这个问题上消除分歧吗？ 在其他所有问题上，他都可能使选民两极分化，他会做到这一点，但是，“我要在后院建一个数据中心，它会发出噪音。” 也许还不够。

但问题是他们不认为这来自特朗普。 他们在想，“这些公司正在进入我们的社区。” 如果你把这些点联系起来，就会发现，“谁支持这些公司？ 总统。 谁给了总统很多钱？ 所有这些不同的公司。”

人们不这么看。 他们认为这些科技寡头只是因为他们的钱而与政治脱节，与任何事物脱节。 他们不认为这与总统有联系。 相反，他们认为这与州长、委员会或其他什么机构有联系。 但特朗普却凌驾于这一切之上。 我不知道为什么。

好吧，我很好奇，也许我们应该到此结束。 佛罗里达州州长初选即将到来。 如果唐纳德输了，即使特朗普在数据中心问题上表示支持，你认为这会是中期选举中会发生什么的信号或预测吗？

我认为这将是一个巨大的信号，哪怕只是因为唐纳德的民意调查比其他人都领先得多。 他是明显的领跑者，而民意调查中排名第二的副州长也支持数据中心。 如果任何反对数据中心的候选人赢得共和党初选，那将是巨大的，并且是该州每个人都完全意想不到的。 但这有可能发生。 更疯狂的事情发生了。

在接下来的几个月里，我们将对此进行大量报道，尤其是在中期选举之前，因为政党路线的混乱、文化战争的混乱似乎非常重要。 我们已经经历了这么长时间的政治，它们似乎无法承受每个人都讨厌同一件事。

也许这就是美国所需要的。 似乎每个美国人都讨厌这些发出巨大噪音的大型建筑，这可能是我们团结起来的原因，这是好事还是坏事。 你可以自己做决定，但我想不到其他的了。 没有什么比这更能跨越党派界限了。 你可以吗？

从字面上看什么也没有。 什么都没有。 我认为，它跨越了党派界限，不仅因为人们讨厌它，而且还让这些极度保守的女性与我谈论当地的环境和生态问题。 他们谈论的是水中的杀虫剂和永久化学物质，看看五到十年前的共和党政治，你不会想到这就是我们的结局。

我们仍在国家层面上进行气候变化骗局，而在实地我们正在谈论农药。 那里有东西。

盖比，随着故事的发展，当然，随着我们进入所有这些选举，我们将不得不让你回来。 非常感谢您来到 Decoder。

是的，谢谢你邀请我。 这很有趣。
